name: Guarana

card.summary: Guarana is an Amazonian seed extract rich in caffeine, used in energy drinks and fat-loss supplements to boost energy and training output.
card.note: High caffeine intake can cause palpitations, anxiety and sleep loss.

quick.overview:
Guarana (Paullinia cupana) is a climbing plant from the Amazon whose seeds can hold up to about 6% caffeine, roughly double to triple green coffee beans [1]. It is a common ingredient in energy drinks and thermogenic or pre-workout supplements.

For looks, the chain is energy and focus, then harder training or a calorie deficit, then a leaner or more muscular physique. Small trials have tested guarana for exercise and cognitive performance.
quick.how: It is taken as a seed powder, extract, capsule or as an ingredient in drinks and stacks, often with other stimulants. Effects are those of caffeine and arrive within about an hour in typical use.
quick.risks: Stimulant effects include jitteriness, raised heart rate, anxiety and sleep disruption. Energy drinks have been linked to serious adverse effects in young people and people with heart conditions [3]. In the US the FDA has not evaluated guarana for GRAS status beyond flavouring use [1].

lead: Guarana (Paullinia cupana) is a climbing plant of the Amazon basin, especially common in Brazil, whose seeds can contain up to about 6 percent caffeine, compared with roughly 1 to 3 percent in green coffee beans.[1] The Sateré-Mawé and Guarani peoples traditionally shell, roast or dry and pound the seeds into a paste shaped into sticks, which is grated into water to make a drink.[1][15]

In fitness and appearance circles guarana is used as a stimulant ingredient in energy drinks, pre-workout powders and thermogenic fat-burner stacks. The chain people describe is alertness and drive, then harder or longer training or a controlled diet, then a leaner or more muscular physique. The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on energy drinks lists guarana among common ingredients and says that the performance benefit of such drinks is largely driven by their caffeine content.[2]

Human research on guarana itself is small and mostly acute: randomised trials on cycling time-trial performance, reaction time, and soccer performance, a pilot in cancer patients with poor appetite, and several studies of multi-ingredient herbal weight-management products that contain guarana.[4][5][9][10][16][17][18] A 2022 narrative review describes the human evidence as limited and calls for more mechanistic work.[6]

chain: Caffeine and other methylxanthines raise alertness
Harder or longer training, or reduced appetite
Greater calorie burn and training volume
angle.text: People take guarana as a stimulant to support training intensity and fat-loss phases. Its effect on appearance is through that extra effort, not a direct change to body tissue.

paras: The plant has large leaves and flower clusters, and its fruit ripens from brown to red and splits to show black seeds partly covered by a white aril, a look often compared to an eye. The name derives from the Sateré-Mawé word for the plant.[1]

Besides caffeine, seeds contain smaller amounts of the xanthines theophylline and theobromine, plus catechins, tannins, starch, protein and resin. Wikipedia lists a caffeine range of roughly 0.9 to 7.6 percent across analyses, and notes that polyphenols can form complexes with caffeine.[1] The caffeine is believed to serve the plant as a defence against insects.[1]

The Sateré-Mawé, who live between the Tapajós and Madeira rivers, are credited with domesticating guarana. A Sateré-Mawé origin myth has a deity plant the eyes of a child, with the left eye giving wild guarana and the right eye the cultivated plant.[1][15] Cultural Survival describes the seed as central to their culture, prepared as çapó, a drink used by hunters and in rituals such as the Festa da Tocandira: seeds are roasted, ground, mixed with manioc and shaped into hard sticks, then grated and dissolved in water.[15]

Plantation varieties yield many times more seeds than the traditional guaraná das terras, which is described as having the best taste and potency; Cultural Survival says this has pressured Mawé producers and that the Brazilian agency FUNAI has backed cooperatives.[15] Wikipedia says guarana was introduced to Europe in the sixteenth century, and a note on guarana appeared in the Buffalo Medical and Surgical Journal in 1874.[1][11]

Guarana is one of the caffeine sources in thermogenic and pre-workout products, and T Nation members mention it in diet and energy-drink discussions.[7][8] The appearance goal is a leaner or more muscular physique reached through extra training effort or diet adherence while alert, rather than through any direct change in tissue.[2]

A 2019 review of off-season nutrition for bodybuilders lists caffeine at 5 to 6 mg/kg among supplements that might yield ergogenic effects, which gives context for why caffeine-containing herbs such as guarana appear in pre-workouts.[19]

Brazil, one of the world's largest soft-drink markets, makes many guarana-flavoured soft drinks, Paraguay produces them too, and in Brazil, Peru and Paraguay the word guaraná often means such a soft drink. A fermented drink of guarana seeds, cassava and water also exists. Guarana is a common source of caffeine for many South Americans and has become a familiar additive in energy drinks worldwide.[1]

A 2024 randomised trial found that guarana, but not a low dose of caffeine, improved cycling time-trial performance compared with placebo.[4] A 2023 double-blind crossover trial of 25 participants compared guarana, caffeine and placebo around maximal cycling: guarana lowered choice reaction time before exercise relative to placebo (407 versus 421 ms) and lowered simple reaction time after exercise (306 versus 323 ms), with no significant difference from caffeine on either measure.[5] A randomised crossover, placebo-controlled study tested acute guarana on soccer player performance.[9]

A 2013 double-blind crossover study in 58 normal to slightly overweight women tested a commercial herbal formulation of yerba mate, guarana and damiana (alone or with inulin fibre) before a test lunch; the formulation was associated with 16.3 percent lower food intake (about 112 kcal) than conditions without it.[16] A 2006 randomised, placebo-controlled trial of 105 overweight adults used a botanical formula containing extracts including guarana and green tea for 12 weeks alongside measured exercise; body fat loss and a body composition index were greater with the formula, while weight, BMI and waist-to-hip ratio did not differ significantly.[17] A 2015 randomised crossover study in 12 recreationally active people tested a nine-herb product containing guarana seed extract and caffeine for effects on fat oxidation, hunger and perceived exertion during cycling.[18] These products combine many ingredients, so effects cannot be assigned to guarana alone.

A pilot phase II trial in advanced cancer patients with appetite loss and weight loss gave a guarana extract for four weeks; of 18 completers, two gained more than 5 percent of body weight and six had at least a three-point appetite improvement, with no significant differences in weight loss or quality of life.[10]

Guarana's effects are those of caffeine. A review of energy drinks in children, adolescents and young adults, which searched the term guarana, reported serious adverse effects in people with seizures, diabetes, cardiac abnormalities or mood and behavioural disorders, said that these drinks often contain high and unregulated amounts of caffeine, and noted that of 5,448 US caffeine overdoses reported in 2007, 46 percent were in people under 19.[3] In the cancer-appetite trial one patient withdrew because of grade II arthralgia, and no grade 3 or 4 toxicities were reported.[10]

In the United States the FDA has not evaluated guarana fruit powder or seed extract for generally-recognised-as-safe status; they are approved as flavouring additives.[1] Brazil's food supplement law officially acknowledges guarana as a source of bioactive compounds.[6] Guarana sits within a wider category of herbal stimulants that includes yerba mate and green tea extract, and fat-burner products often combine it with other caffeine sources and ingredients.[16][18]

Randomised trials have tested guarana on cycling performance, reaction times and soccer performance,[4][5][9] a crossover study tested a guarana-containing herbal formulation on appetite and food intake,[16] a randomised trial tested a botanical weight-management formula that contained guarana,[17] and a pilot trial examined guarana in cancer patients with poor appetite.[10] A narrative review summarises the human evidence as limited.[6]

lore.intro: Guarana comes up in gym and diet forums mainly as a caffeine source inside fat burners, pre-workouts and energy drinks.[7][8]

claims.claim: Guarana gives longer-lasting, stronger energy than ordinary caffeine.
claims.believers: Proponents point to the seed's high caffeine content and to its polyphenols and other compounds as making the effect different from coffee.[1]
claims.experts: A 2024 cycling trial found guarana improved time-trial performance where low-dose caffeine did not, while a 2023 trial found guarana's cognitive effects did not differ significantly from caffeine.[4][5] The ISSN position stand attributes energy-drink performance effects largely to caffeine.[2]

claims.claim: Guarana helps with fat loss when stacked in a fat burner.
claims.believers: Forum members list it among the stimulants in thermogenic and cutting discussions.[7][8]
claims.experts: Trials of multi-ingredient products containing guarana report effects on body fat, hunger or fat oxidation, but they combine several ingredients.[17][18] No published trial has tested guarana alone for body composition in healthy adults.

claims.believers: Proponents of stimulant herbal blends describe feeling less hungry on them.[16]
claims.experts: A crossover study of a yerba mate, guarana and damiana formulation found lower food intake at a test lunch,[16] and a pilot in advanced cancer patients found small appetite improvements in some participants.[10]

claims.claim: Because it is a plant, guarana is a gentler stimulant than synthetic ones.
claims.believers: Natural-product framing presents herbal stimulants as milder.[1]
claims.experts: Its effects come largely from caffeine, and a pediatric review reported serious adverse effects from caffeine-rich energy drinks in vulnerable groups.[3] The FDA has not evaluated guarana for GRAS status.[1]
